title: Nobody Asked for This: How Mild Preferences Build a Segregated City
audience: A curious adult with no background in this field

source.title: Understanding the social context of the Schelling segregation model
source.authors: William A V Clark, Mark Fossett
source.venue: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences (PNAS)

intro.summary: This lesson draws on four sources about Thomas Schelling's segregation model: an encyclopedia overview, Clark and Fossett's 2008 PNAS paper on its social meaning, Gauvin, Vannimenus and Nadal's physics-style phase diagram, and Rogers and McKane's unified mathematical framework. They ask one question: can households that are content to live in mixed neighbourhoods still produce a highly segregated city with no outside force pushing them apart? Simulations, formal proofs and survey data all say yes. Once the share of like neighbours people want reaches their group's share of the city, small moves trigger a chain of further moves, and neighbourhoods drift toward being all one group. The result holds across many versions of the model. The main limitation is that these are toy worlds. They show that preferences could produce segregation, not that preferences do produce it in real cities, where discrimination, income and history also act, and where the authors stress that separate effects are hard to measure. The lesson leaves out cluster-size and entropy measures, the physics analogies in depth (Ising and Blume–Capel models), Schelling games from game theory, and income or price extensions. These are good follow-up topics.
background: An agent-based model is a computer simulation where many simple 'agents' each follow a rule, and we watch what pattern the whole group forms.
In Schelling's model, households are coloured squares on a grid, and each one looks at its eight surrounding squares to decide whether to stay or move.
De facto segregation means separation that arises from people's own choices and moves, rather than from laws that require it.
Through the 1980s and 1990s, social scientists debated whether US residential segregation came mainly from housing discrimination or partly from household preferences.
intro.aha: Households who would be perfectly happy as a minority on their street still sort themselves into a city far more segregated than any of them wanted, so in these models tolerance alone does not bring integration.

primer.heading: The question
primer.body: Many cities are sharply divided by race or ethnicity. One easy explanation is that people strongly dislike living near other groups, or are forced apart. In 1971 the economist Thomas Schelling asked a quieter question: what if people are only mildly picky? Suppose they would happily be a minority on their street, as long as they are not almost alone. Could the city still end up split?
primer.quote: Schelling's work does demonstrate that having people with "mild" in-group preference towards their own group could still lead to a highly segregated society via de facto segregation.

primer.heading: What they did
primer.body: Schelling placed two colours of households at random on a grid with some empty squares. Each household looked at its neighbours. If too few were its own colour, it moved to an empty square. Later researchers built on this. Clark and Fossett ran a richer city simulation with three groups, house quality and income, using preference levels taken from real Los Angeles surveys. Gauvin and colleagues mapped which settings give mixed, segregated or 'frozen' cities. Rogers and McKane showed that five quite different versions of the model segregate along the same curve, and they wrote a simple equation that fits that curve.

primer.heading: What they found
primer.body: With two equal groups, the city stays mixed if households want fewer than about a third of their neighbours to be like them. Above that, it segregates strongly. The key point is a tipping rule: segregation takes off once the share of like neighbours people want reaches their group's share of the city. The reason is a feedback loop. Each move makes the old neighbourhood less attractive to the mover's group and the new one less attractive to the other group, which triggers more moves.
primer.quote: The resulting neighborhood structure is more segregated than most individual households would find “ideal.”

primer.heading: Why it matters, and its limits
primer.body: If mild preferences alone can sort a city, then ending discrimination may not bring quick integration. Clark and Fossett argue this, while noting that the fixes for preferences would be very different from anti-discrimination law. There are big caveats. The models show what could happen, not what did happen in any real city. Several causes act at once and are hard to separate with real data. Rogers and McKane quote Schelling's own warning that the model's numbers refer to an artificial checkerboard. Scholars who stress housing discrimination dispute how much weight preferences deserve.
primer.quote: They suggest that mere tolerance and the absence of virulent housing discrimination will not produce integration under prevailing patterns of ethnic preference, at least, not in the short run.

concepts.title: One household's rule: stay or move
concepts.idea: A household stays if the share of its occupied neighbouring squares holding its own group meets its required share, and moves otherwise.

predict.question: A household needs at least one third of its neighbours to be alike. Around it are 2 alike neighbours, 4 unlike neighbours and 2 empty squares. What does it do?
options: It stays: 2 of its 6 occupied neighbours is exactly one third
It moves: 2 of 8 squares is only a quarter
It moves: unlike neighbours outnumber alike ones
It waits until the empty squares fill up before deciding
why: Correct. Empty squares are ignored, so the share alike is 2 out of 6 occupied neighbours. That equals one third, and meeting the threshold is enough to stay.
Tempting if you count the empty squares, but the rule ignores them. Only the 6 squares that hold someone are counted.
Being outnumbered feels like it should matter, but the rule only compares the share alike with the threshold. One third alike meets a one-third threshold, even as a local minority.
The rule is checked against the neighbours who are there now. Empty squares neither help nor hurt until someone moves in.

terms.means: The share of alike neighbours a household requires before it is content to stay, written B_a
Wanting at least some of your neighbours to be from your own group
The eight squares around a square on the grid: up, down, left, right and the four diagonals

model.title: One household and its eight neighbouring squares
model.note: Teaching model: one household, its eight surrounding squares, and a single stay-or-move check. It follows the rule as Wikipedia describes Schelling's model: empty squares are ignored, and the household stays if the share alike B is at least its requirement B_a. Variants differ. Schelling's original used 'half or more' alike, as Clark and Fossett describe it. Gauvin et al. state the rule as a cap on unlike neighbours. If alike neighbours plus empty squares would exceed 8, the empty count is trimmed to fit. Numbers are illustrative, not data from any paper.

steps.say: Picture one household on a city grid, with eight squares around it.
This slider sets how many neighbours belong to the household's own group. The rest belong to the other group.
This slider leaves some squares empty. Empty squares count for neither group.
The left bar shows what share of the neighbours actually there are alike.
The right bar is how much alike the household wants. The last box says whether it stays or moves.

explore.prompt: Play with the household's surroundings and its demands. Find exactly where 'stay' flips to 'move'.

goals.text: Keep the requirement at half or more, and make the household content even though it has fewer than 4 alike neighbours.
hints: Alike neighbours stay below 4 here. What else changes the share alike?
Empty squares drop out of the count. Try leaving some neighbouring squares empty.
You need as many alike as unlike among the neighbours who are actually there.

goals.text: With 3 alike and 5 unlike neighbours and no empty squares, raise the requirement as high as it can go while the household still stays.
hints: Leave the neighbours as they are and work only on the requirement.
The household stays while its requirement is at or below its share alike. What is 3 out of 8 as a percentage?
The highest whole-percent requirement sits just under 3/8 written as a percentage.

feedback.correct: Right. Empty squares are ignored, so the share alike is 2 of 6 occupied neighbours, exactly one third. Meeting the threshold is enough, so the household stays even though its group is the local minority.
feedback.incorrect: The rule counts only occupied neighbouring squares and asks one question: is the share alike at least the threshold? Here it is 2 of 6, which is one third, so the household stays.

steps.say: Start with Schelling's original rule: the household wants half or more of its neighbours alike. With 4 alike and 4 unlike, the share is exactly 50%, so it stays.
Swap one alike neighbour for an unlike one. Now 3 of 8 is 37.5%, below the bar, and the household moves.
The household's requirement is called its threshold, written B_a. Wanting some neighbours from your own group is called in-group preference.
The eight squares around it form its Moore neighbourhood. Now leave two of them empty. Only 6 occupied squares are counted, and 3 of 6 is 50%, so the household stays.
Fill the empty squares with unlike neighbours again, and lower the threshold to one third, the level some later studies use.
Now 3 alike of 8 is 37.5%. That clears one third, so the household stays.
Drop to 2 alike: 25% is below one third, so it moves.
Back to 3 alike. With a one-third threshold, this household is content even though its own group is the minority around it. That is a very mild wish.

understand.explanation: Schelling's model gives each household one simple test. It looks at its neighbouring squares and ignores the empty ones. Then it works out what share of the rest belong to its own group. If that share meets its threshold, it stays. If not, it moves to a vacant spot that would satisfy it. In Schelling's original version the threshold was half or more alike. Later variants, such as the one Gauvin and colleagues study, use one third, where 3 alike out of 8 is already enough. This is a teaching rule, not a portrait of real families: real households also weigh price, schools and much more.
understand.quote: It posited that an agent, a model representation of a household that could be white or black, preferred to be on a square on a checkerboard in which half or more of the eight adjacent neighbors were of a similar color. In the economic context, this was seen as having utility one compared with having utility zero.
understand.quote_where: Introduction (unnumbered), paragraph on the original Schelling agent model

connect.caption: This is the model's rule written out; Wikipedia states it in words with the same symbols. B, the left bar, is the share of occupied neighbours from the household's own group, with empty squares left out of the bottom of the fraction. B_a, the right bar, is the household's threshold. The household stays when B is at least B_a, and otherwise moves to a vacant spot that would satisfy it.

concepts.recap: Each household compares the share alike among its occupied neighbours with its threshold: at or above, it stays; below, it moves.

concepts.title: Why one move triggers the next
concepts.idea: When a household leaves a mixed area for one where its group is larger, both neighbourhoods tilt further toward one group, which makes more households unhappy and sets off more moves.

terms.means: A chain where the result of one step feeds back and causes more of the same step

concepts.recap: Every move takes a like neighbour away from the people left behind and adds an unlike neighbour for the other group where it lands, so one move can push others below their rule and set off the next.

understand.explanation: In the last concept, one household followed a simple rule: stay if enough of its neighbours are like it, and move if not. But a move is never private. When a household leaves a mixed area for one where its group is larger, it takes one like neighbour away from the people it left behind. Where it arrives, it adds one unlike neighbour for the other group. Some of those people may now fall below their own required share and move too, which tilts more areas and unsettles more households. This is a feedback loop: each step's result feeds the next step. Clark and Fossett describe this loop in the standard two-group model and note that it stops only if most households strongly dislike being in the majority. It is a mechanism shown in models, not on its own proof of how real neighbourhoods change.
understand.quote: The neighborhood they leave becomes less attractive to members of their group and the neighborhood they enter becomes less attractive to members of the other group. Over successive iterations, homogeneous neighborhoods emerge.
understand.quote_where: Section 'Preferences, Tolerance, and the Basis of Simulation Models'

activities.title: One move on a small patch of the city

steps.text: Set the rule. Every household wants at least half of its occupied neighbouring squares to hold its own group. This is the 'half or more' rule from Schelling's original checkerboard. Empty squares don't count.
Household M is Blue and lives in area A. Of its 8 neighbours, 3 are Blue and 5 are Orange.
M moves into an empty square in area B. Its new neighbours are 5 Blue and 3 Orange.
steps.result: 5 of 8 = 62.5%, so M is now content

steps.text: Back in A, Blue household X was one of M's neighbours. Before the move, X had 4 Blue and 4 Orange neighbours, and M was one of the Blues. M's square is now empty.
steps.result: Before: 4/8 = 50%, so X stays. After: 3/7 ≈ 43%, so X now wants to move

steps.text: In B, Orange household Y sits beside M's new square. Before the move, Y had 3 Orange and 3 Blue neighbours, plus 2 empty squares. One of those empty squares now holds M.
steps.result: Before: 3/6 = 50%, so Y stays. After: 3/7 ≈ 43%, so Y now wants to move

steps.text: One unhappy household has become two. If X moves to a more Blue area and Y to a more Orange one, each of those moves can unsettle someone else in the same way.

activities.takeaway: M's move solved M's own problem, but it pushed one Blue in A and one Orange in B below the line. Neither X nor Y changed what they wanted. Their neighbourhood changed around them.

activities.question: Stay with the same patch. Besides X and Y, M's move changed the neighbourhood for other households too. Select every group whose share of like neighbours went DOWN because of the move.

options.text: Orange households in A, next to M's old square
options.feedback: Not these. They lost an unlike (Blue) neighbour. With fewer Blues counted around them, their Orange share stays the same or rises. Area A tilts toward Orange, which suits them.

options.text: Blue households in A, next to M's old square
options.feedback: Yes. They lost a like neighbour, just as X did. The area they live in becomes less attractive to their own group, so some of them may now fall below 1/2.

options.text: Orange households in B, next to M's new square
options.feedback: Yes. They gained an unlike neighbour, just as Y did. The area M entered becomes less attractive to the other group, so some Oranges there may now fall below 1/2.

options.text: Blue households in B, next to M's new square
options.feedback: Not these. They gained a like neighbour, so their Blue share rises. Area B tilts toward Blue, which suits them and makes it more appealing to other Blues.

hints: For each group, ask: did it lose a neighbour like itself, or gain a neighbour unlike itself?
M is Blue. Removing a Blue hurts the Blues left behind, and adding a Blue hurts the Oranges where M lands.

activities.prompt: Trace the route the moving rule takes, from one unhappy household to areas made up mostly of one group. Follow the arrows and skip the dead ends.

nodes.label: A household is below its required share
It moves where its group is larger
Both areas tilt toward one group
Everyone is content after one move
More households fall below their share

activities.explanation: The move goes toward the household's own group, so it makes areas less mixed, not more. Each move tilts both the old and the new area, which pushes other households below their share, so contentment does not arrive after one move. Those households then move, and the arrow from 'move too' back to 'tilt' is the feedback loop that repeats. Clark and Fossett note that the drift toward one group stops only if most households strongly dislike being in the majority, and surveys suggest few do. This chain shows how preferences could drive segregation. It does not show that this is the only cause in real cities.
hints: Ask whether a move toward your own group makes either area more mixed.
One of the arrows loops back: moves cause tilting, and tilting causes more moves.

concepts.title: The tipping line: wanting more than your group's share
concepts.idea: In a perfectly mixed city each household's like share equals its group's share of the city, so everyone can be satisfied only while the required share stays at or below that group share.

predict.question: A new city has three groups making up 65%, 25% and 10% of households. Every household wants at least 30% like neighbours. If this city were perfectly mixed, which groups would be left discontent?
options: Nobody, because 30% is a mild wish
why: The smallest group stands out, but the 25% group also gets only 25% like neighbours in a mixed city, which is still below the 30% it wants.
Correct: in a perfectly mixed city each household's like share equals its group's share. 10% and 25% both fall short of 30%, and only the 65% group clears it.
Whether a wish is mild depends on the group's size. 30% is easy for a group that is 65% of the city and impossible to meet by mixing for groups of 25% or 10%.
The big group is the one with room to spare: mixing gives it 65% like neighbours, far above 30%. The trouble is with the smaller groups.

terms.means: The share of like neighbours a household is aiming for before it is content
A group's share of all the households in the city
A perfectly mixed city, where every neighbourhood has the same group mix as the city as a whole

model.title: Like neighbours you'd get in a perfectly mixed city vs. like neighbours wanted
model.note: Teaching model: it assumes a perfectly mixed city where every household's neighbourhood exactly matches the citywide mix, and that every household in the group wants the same share. Real neighbourhoods are small and their mix wobbles around the city average, so this shows only the arithmetic ceiling, not what a simulation would do. The 33%, 20% and 40% figures are Clark and Fossett's simulation settings. Other numbers are illustrative.

controls.label: Your group's share of the city

outputs.label: Everyone in the group content? (1 yes, 0 no)

bars.label: Like neighbours in a perfectly mixed city

steps.say: Picture a city where every neighbourhood has exactly the same mix of groups as the whole city.
This slider sets how big your group is. In that mixed city, your like neighbours simply equal your group's share, so the first bar follows it.
This slider sets how many like neighbours each household wants. That is the second bar.
These boxes show how much room is left over, and whether everyone in the group would be content.
Let's go back to the city from the paper.

explore.prompt: Find the line where a perfectly mixed city stops working for this group, from both sides: by changing the wish, then by changing the group's size.

goals.text: Leave the group at one third of the city. Make the wish just too strict for a perfectly mixed city, using the smallest step past the line that you can.
hints: Which bar has to end up taller than the other for the mixed city to fail?
Raise the wish one notch at a time and watch the content box.
Stop at the first notch where the second bar just pokes above the first.

goals.text: Put the wish back where it started and leave it there. Change the group's size so a perfectly mixed city contents the group with nothing at all to spare.
hints: Room to spare is the gap between the two bars.
Move the group-size slider, not the wish.
You want the first bar exactly level with the second.

feedback.correct: Right. A mixed city hands every household its group's share of like neighbours, so any group smaller than 30% falls short. Clark and Fossett note that unequal group sizes like 65/25/10 produced higher segregation in their simulations than equal groups did.
feedback.incorrect: The test is not whether a wish sounds mild. It is whether the wish fits under the group's share of the city. In a perfectly mixed city the 25% and 10% groups get only 25% and 10% like neighbours, both short of 30%. Clark and Fossett report higher segregation with a 65/25/10 split than with equal groups.

steps.say: Here is Clark and Fossett's city: three equal groups, each about one third. Each household wants 20% like neighbours. In a perfectly mixed city it gets 33%, so it is content with 13 points to spare.
The paper calls that 20% wish a preference target: the share of like neighbours a household is aiming for.
Raise the target to 30%. It is still under 33%, so mixing still works, but the spare room has shrunk to 3 points.

Now 40%, close to what surveys find. The wanted bar passes the mixed-city bar. In a perfectly mixed city nobody in this group gets what they want, and with three equal groups that means nobody at all.

The group's share of the city is its population representation. A city where every neighbourhood matches that mix is an even distribution. The line sits where the target equals the population representation.

Make the group 40% of the city with a 40% target. The bars are level: content, with zero to spare. Any wobble in a real neighbourhood would push some under, and the paper counts reaching the share as tipping.
Same 40% target, bigger group: at half the city the bar clears it easily. Whether a wish can be met by mixing depends on the group's size, not just on the wish.

understand.explanation: If a city is perfectly mixed, every household's share of like neighbours is simply its group's share of the city. So mixing can satisfy a group only while its target is no higher than that share. Clark and Fossett used this to explain their three-group simulations, with each group about a third of the city. Targets of 20% left segregation low, because households could be content in neighbourhoods that matched the city's mix. Targets of 40% or more sent it high. This is only a ceiling: real neighbourhoods are small and never exactly match the citywide average, so a city can drift apart even below the line, and the simulations also built in income and housing-quality goals.
understand.quote: The crucial transition occurs when preference targets reach or exceed a group's population representation (22). Thus, high levels of segregation emerge when targets for same-group contact shift from 20% to 40%. Segregation is low when households seek 20% same-group contact because all households can be satisfied in neighborhoods that match the city's ethnic mix.

equation.text: everyone content in a perfectly mixed city

connect.caption: This is the model's rule; the paper states it in words, not as an equation. The second bar is the preference target and the first is the population representation. The content box turns to 1 exactly when the target fits under the group's share.

concepts.recap: A perfectly mixed city can content a group only if the share of like neighbours it wants is no bigger than the group's share of the city.

concepts.title: Mild wishes, segregated city
concepts.idea: Running the moving rule across a whole grid makes neighbourhoods far more alike than anyone required, and the jump starts near a required share of about one third for two equal groups.

predict.question: Clark and Fossett also simulated a city with three equal-sized groups instead of two. Suppose every household there asks for 40% like neighbours, a little above what tipped our two-group city. What would you expect?
options: It stays mixed: 40% still means accepting a minority of like neighbours, so it is a mild wish
It sorts into clusters: 40% is more than each group's one-third share of the city
It sorts, but only about half as much as a two-group city, because three groups dilute each other
Nothing can be said without knowing the households' incomes
why: The wish does sound mild. But with three equal groups, a mixed neighbourhood gives each household only about a third like neighbours, so 40% cannot be met everywhere and moves cascade.

Right. In a mixed three-group city each household's like share is about one third. A 40% target is above that, so not everyone can be content in a mix. Clark and Fossett saw high segregation emerge at 40%, but not at 20%.

More groups do not soften the effect. Each group is a smaller share of the city, so the same target is harder to meet in a mix. Clark and Fossett found minorities ended up apart from the majority and also from each other.

Their simulated households did have incomes and housing-quality goals, weighted equally with the neighbour goal. Ethnic segregation still jumped at 40%, so the preference alone was enough to drive it.

terms.means: A pattern of the whole city that no single household asked for or would choose on its own

model.title: A city of two groups sorting itself
model.note: Teaching model: a 30 × 30 grid with two equal groups and about 10% empty squares, starting from a random mix. Each round, every household with fewer like neighbours than required (as a share of its occupied neighbouring squares) moves to a random empty square. The run lasts up to 100 rounds. This is close to, but not the same as, the papers' variants. Schelling moved households to the nearest square that satisfied them. Gauvin et al. let content households move too, but only into squares that satisfy them, which can freeze the city at very strict demands; this model does not show that. Numbers are illustrative, not the papers' data.

outputs.label: Neighbours who are like me (city average)
More alike than a random mix
Households still unhappy at the end

steps.say: Each square is a home. The two colours are two equal-sized groups, and blank squares are empty. The run starts with everyone scattered at random.
This slider sets the share of like neighbours every household wants. A household below it packs up and moves to a random empty square.
This box shows the end result: on average, what share of a household's neighbours are its own colour.
This one compares that with a random mix, which gives about 50% for two equal groups.
And this one counts households still unhappy when the run stops.

explore.prompt: Play with the requirement. Look for where the city stays a random jumble, where it suddenly sorts, and how far the result overshoots the wish.

goals.text: Make households genuinely choosy (a requirement above 10%) while the city still ends up close to a random mix: like share under 60%.
hints: Think about where the switch sits for two equal groups.
Stay clearly below one third. There, only a few unlucky households fall short, and their moves don't set off a chain.
Try something between a tenth and a quarter.

goals.text: Get neighbourhoods at least three-quarters alike, while no household asks for more than half of its neighbours to be like it.
hints: Crossing the switch sorts the city. Going further past it sorts the city a bit more.
The lowest setting that tips may not reach three-quarters. Look higher in the allowed range.
Stay at or under one half, near the top of that limit.

feedback.correct: Yes. The switch comes when the required share can't be met by everyone in a mixed city. With three equal groups that happens above about one third, so 40% sorts the city. Clark and Fossett saw high segregation emerge when targets rose from 20% to 40%.
feedback.incorrect: The trap is judging the wish by how mild it sounds. What matters is whether the city's own mix can satisfy it. With three equal groups a mixed neighbourhood offers each household only about a third like neighbours. A 40% target can't be met everywhere, so moves cascade, and Clark and Fossett saw high segregation emerge at 40%.

steps.say: Start with households that don't care at all. Nobody moves, and the like share sits near 50%, which is just what a random mix of two equal groups gives.
Now each household wants at least a fifth of its neighbours to be like it. By chance a few fall short and move, but the city barely changes. It still looks like a jumble.
Raise it to a quarter. Still little change: with about seven neighbours, very few households have only one like neighbour or none.

Now go to about one third. A random city is lumpier than a perfectly mixed one, so quite a few households now fall short. Each move tilts two neighbourhoods, and the chain you met earlier takes off. Watch clusters form.

When it settles, nearly everyone is content, yet neighbourhoods are far more alike than the one third anyone asked for. That gap is an emergent effect: a pattern of the whole city that no household demanded.
Push the requirement much higher. The city sorts a little more, but the big switch from jumble to clusters already happened near one third.

Come back to one third and look again. These households would accept being outnumbered by their neighbours, yet they live in a city of clusters. Schelling found this switch at about one third for two equal groups.

understand.explanation: Run the one-household rule across a whole grid, and the city ends up far more alike than anyone asked for. A random start is not perfectly mixed: by chance some households have fewer like neighbours than others. Once the requirement nears one third, enough of them fall short to set off the chain of moves. Schelling found that for two equal groups the city stays random below about one third and sorts itself above it. Gauvin and colleagues mapped sharp switches between mixed and segregated states in their variant. Clark and Fossett saw a three-group city segregate when targets rose from 20% to 40%, with little extra change from raising them further. The exact switch point depends on rule details such as vacancies and how households search, and these are models: they show what mild preferences can produce, not what caused segregation in any real city.
understand.quote: The crucial point is that segregation appears as an emergent phenomenon, in the sense that the collective eﬀect is much stronger than what would be naively expected, as individual agents are happy to live in a mixed neighborhood.

check.task: Put the model in the state of Schelling's headline finding: a requirement no stricter than 35%, yet neighbourhoods end up at least two-thirds alike.
check.hint: Below about a quarter, the city stays a jumble. Look between a quarter and the 35% cap, where the chain of moves takes off.
check.misconception: That a strongly sorted city must come from households who strongly want to live among their own group.

connect.caption: In Wikipedia's notation, B is one household's share of like neighbours (ignoring empty squares), and B_a is the share it requires: the slider. A household relocates when B < B_a. The final city average of B (the like-share box) ends up far above B_a once B_a passes about one third. The '≫' is the model's lesson, not part of the paper's rule.

concepts.recap: Mild individual wishes, about one third like neighbours for two equal groups, can sort a whole city far more than anyone asked for.

activities.prompt: Three cities, identical except for how many like neighbours households require. Compare the like share and the picture in each.
activities.takeaway: The big change, from jumble to clusters, happens crossing roughly one third. Above that, this model sorts a little further. Clark and Fossett likewise report that raising targets past the critical level had minimal additional impact on their segregation index.

concepts.title: Same curve, many models: a slight bias is enough
concepts.idea: Rogers and McKane's simple equation shows that when unlike neighbour pairs are broken up faster than they form, the share of unlike pairs falls steeply and then levels off, and this one curve fits five quite different Schelling-type models.

predict.question: Imagine a variant in which a broken-up mixed pair never forms again: the forming rate is exactly zero, while the break-up rate stays positive. What does the equation predict for the share of unlike pairs?
options: It keeps falling toward zero, but more and more slowly
It levels off at about 0.06, like the paper's fit
It stays at 0.5, because nothing new forms
It drops to zero almost at once
why: Correct. With nothing forming, only the break-up term is left, so the share can only shrink. The paper notes it then falls like 1/t: always heading for zero, never quite arriving.
Tempting, because the fit levels off there. But that plateau is where forming and breaking up balance. With no forming at all there is nothing to balance, so there is no plateau above zero.
Nothing new forms, but existing mixed pairs still break up at rate β. So the share must fall. It only stays at 0.5 when the two rates are equal.
Break-ups happen at a finite rate, and fewer mixed pairs are left to break as the share falls. So the fall slows down rather than happening in one jump.

terms.means: Out of all pairs of next-door neighbours, the share that belong to different groups. 0.5 means randomly mixed; near 0 means sorted.
The level the curve settles at, where mixed pairs form and break up equally often
A deliberately stripped-down model whose simple equation still reproduces what bigger, messier models do

model.title: How the share of mixed neighbour pairs falls over time
model.note: Teaching model: this plots the paper's exact solution for its stripped-down pair model (each site has one neighbour, there are no empty sites, and agents swap places). It is not the five full simulations. Time is in the paper's rescaled units. The slider ranges are illustrative. Only the dashed curve (α = 0.0002, β = 0.05) is the authors' fitted result.

controls.label: How fast mixed pairs break up (β)

outputs.label: Break-ups happen this many times faster
Share of mixed pairs at time 100

y.label: Share of neighbour pairs that are mixed

steps.say: This curve tracks one number over time. Take every pair of next-door neighbours: what share of those pairs come from different groups?
It starts at 0.5. That is what you get when the two groups are scattered at random.
This slider sets how fast new mixed pairs form as people move around.
This one sets how fast mixed pairs break up. Push it up and watch the curve.
The dashed curve is the fit the authors found for five published versions of Schelling's model.

explore.prompt: Play with the two rates. Notice that one thing decides where the curve settles and another decides how fast it gets there.

goals.text: Make the long-run share of mixed pairs settle below 0.2
hints: What decides where the curve ends: how big the rates are, or how they compare?
Watch the 'this many times faster' box while you move both sliders.
The long-run share drops under 0.2 once break-ups are well over ten times as fast as forming.

goals.text: Keep the authors' long-run level (a final share between 0.05 and 0.07), but make segregation arrive faster: below 0.12 by time 100
hints: The final level depends only on the ratio of the two rates. Speed depends on something else.
Keep the ratio near the authors' value, but make both rates bigger together.
Scale both of the authors' rates up by the same factor. The break-up slider can't go much past double their value.

feedback.correct: Right. With the forming rate at zero, only break-ups remain, so the mixed share can only shrink. The paper says it then falls like 1/t: always toward zero, ever more slowly, with no plateau above zero.
feedback.incorrect: The plateau you saw is a balance between forming and breaking up. Remove forming entirely and nothing balances the break-ups. The share keeps falling toward zero. It slows down because fewer mixed pairs are left to break, but it never stops at a fixed level above zero.

steps.say: Start with the two rates equal. Mixed pairs break up exactly as often as they form, so the share stays at 0.5. This share of mixed pairs has a name: the interface density.
Make break-ups twice as common as forming. The curve dips, then levels off near 0.41. A mild imbalance in rates gives mild sorting.
Now make forming very rare: break-ups are 50 times as common. The curve sinks a long way, but slowly. It is still falling at the right edge.
These are the authors' fitted values: α = 0.0002, β = 0.05. Your curve now sits on the dashed one: a steep early fall, then a long flattening near 0.06.
The level where it flattens is the equilibrium. Its height depends only on the ratio of the two rates, here 250.
Halve both rates. The ratio is unchanged, so the curve ends at the same level, but it gets there more slowly. The ratio sets where it ends; the overall size of the rates sets how fast.
Back to the fit. The authors call this an effective theory: a toy model of pairs whose one equation tracks how segregation first emerges in five much richer models.

understand.explanation: Rogers and McKane simulated five published Schelling-type models with different grids, networks, satisfaction rules and moving rules, and tracked the interface density. For short to medium times, after rescaling and shifting time to line the runs up, all five fell along one characteristic curve. That includes a model whose agents would be happiest in a mixed area. They then built a stripped-down pair model whose interface density obeys one equation, with α the rate mixed pairs form and β the rate they break up. With α = 0.0002 and β = 0.05 it fits all five. In the pair model those rates mean agents are only 0.0249 more satisfied with a like neighbour than an unlike one, though the authors note this gap looks small partly because each site has just one neighbour. The fit covers only the early emergence of segregation: at long times the models disagree. Like any checkerboard measure, it says nothing directly about real cities.
understand.quote: Simulation results for the time evolution of interface density in five different models taken from several disciplines were presented, each displaying the same characteristic form in short to medium timescales.

connect.caption: This is the paper's equation (7). x is the interface density (the curve). α (blue slider) adds mixed pairs, and does so most when few remain; β (orange slider) removes them, and does so most when many remain. The curve settles where the two terms cancel: x = 1/(1 + √(β/α)), the 'long-run share' box. The paper writes α = 2(1 − u)v and β = 2(1 − v)u, where u and v are an agent's satisfaction with a like and an unlike neighbour.

concepts.recap: If mixed pairs break up faster than they form, their share falls steeply and then levels off, and one such curve fits the early stage of five quite different Schelling models.

activities.prompt: How the authors showed that very different models share one curve, step by step.

stages.label: Five rulebooks
stages.text: Schelling's original grid; Pancs and Vriend's 'best response' agents, whose happiness actually peaks in a mixed neighbourhood; Gauvin et al.'s random jumpers who tolerate up to 60% unlike neighbours; Laurie and Jaggi's agents who look two squares away; and Fagiolo et al.'s agents on a small-world network. Each run had 10,000 sites with 10% empty.

stages.label: One yardstick
stages.text: For each run they tracked a single number over time: the share of neighbour pairs that are mixed. Time was rescaled for system size and shifted so the curves could be compared.

stages.label: One curve
stages.text: Despite their different rules, all five fell along a single characteristic curve until the mixed share dropped below about 0.1, by which point the grid is already strongly segregated. Even agents who prefer mixed areas segregated.

stages.label: Where they part
stages.text: At long times the models disagree. Some freeze in a fixed layout, while others keep reshuffling around a steady state. The shared curve covers only the emergence of segregation.

stages.label: One equation
stages.text: A toy model with one neighbour per site, no empty squares and simple swaps gives an exact equation for the curve. With α = 0.0002 and β = 0.05 it traces all five simulations over four powers of ten in time.

activities.takeaway: The steep early fall in mixed pairs does not depend on the fine print of the rules. It looks like a generic result of mixed pairs breaking up faster than they form, even when the underlying preference gap is slight.

concepts.title: What the model shows, and what it doesn't
concepts.idea: The models and surveys show that preferences alone could produce and sustain segregation even without discrimination, which challenges the hope of quick integration. They do not prove that preferences are the main cause in real cities.

terms.means: How strongly people prefer neighbours from their own group over neighbours from other groups
Data observed in real cities, where causes such as discrimination, income and preferences all act at once and cannot be switched on and off one at a time
An arrangement that a random process keeps returning to and staying near over the long run, whatever it started from

concepts.recap: Models show preferences could create and sustain segregation without discrimination, so tolerance alone may not integrate a city. They can't measure how much preferences cause in real cities.

understand.explanation: The models and surveys establish a possibility, not a verdict. Formal proofs show that segregation is a stochastically stable state: a Schelling-type housing market keeps returning to it and stays there. Simulations add that preferences for similar neighbours, which the paper calls social distance, can create segregation with no discrimination at all, at the strengths people report in surveys. That is why Clark and Fossett doubt that ending discrimination alone would bring quick integration. Real cities, though, give only nonexperimental evidence: discrimination, income gaps and preferences act together and cannot be switched off one at a time, so the models cannot say how much of real segregation each one causes. Rogers and McKane add a warning that numbers from an artificial grid need great care before they are read as facts about real societies.
understand.quote: The visual outcomes and quantitative results constitute powerful evidence that social distance and preference dynamics do have the logical capacity to combine with socioeconomic inequality between groups to create relatively high levels of ethnic and class segregation.

activities.prompt: Clark and Fossett build their case in layers. Reveal each layer, and notice both what it adds and where it stops.

stages.label: 1. The debate they enter
stages.text: Through the 1980s, most social scientists explained residential segregation mainly by housing discrimination, principally by white residents. Clark and Fossett ask a narrower question: could social distance alone generate and sustain segregation even with no discrimination? They also stress that law treats the two differently. Discrimination is illegal and has legal remedies, while preferences are voluntary choices that fair-housing law does not reach.

stages.label: 2. Mathematical proofs
stages.text: Zhang proved that in a Schelling-type housing market, segregation is a stochastically stable state. The model drifts back to it and stays there, whatever the starting arrangement, even with no discrimination and even when only one group has a mild preference. In his case white agents had a modest preference for white neighbours (around 60–70%) and black agents were neutral. This shows segregation is possible. It does not show how often it happens in reality.

stages.label: 3. What people say they want
stages.text: In a Los Angeles survey, people filled in an 'ideal' neighbourhood grid. The share choosing at least 3 of their 8 nearest neighbours from their own group was 60% for Black respondents, 66% for Hispanic, 72% for white and 75% for Asian respondents. No group preferred being a minority, so no single neighbourhood mix could satisfy every group at once. These are stated wishes in one city, not observed moves.

stages.label: 4. Three-group simulations
stages.text: The authors' SimSeg model ran 500 replications of each design for a city with three equal-sized groups. When households wanted 20% of their neighbours from their own group, segregation stayed low. At 40%, close to survey levels, it rose fast and stayed high, and raising the target further changed little. Minority groups also ended up separated from each other, which theories of white discrimination do not predict. The authors note that equal group sizes are the setting most favourable to integration.

stages.label: 5. Where the evidence stops
stages.text: Real cities give only nonexperimental evidence, so neither side of the debate can measure how much preferences or discrimination actually contribute. The authors agree that several factors probably act together. In their simulations, one factor's apparent effect is large when it is the only one switched on, but usually small when others are already active. Rogers and McKane also warn that numbers from an artificial checkerboard need great care before being applied to real societies.

stages.label: 6. Why tolerance is not enough
stages.text: In every group, a sizeable share of respondents would accept fewer same-group neighbours. About 40% of Black respondents, for example, chose fewer than 3 of 8. Yet every household that arrives makes a neighbourhood more attractive to its own group and less attractive to the others. Unless most households actively avoid being in the majority, and the surveys say they don't, neighbourhoods drift toward sameness. The final pattern is more segregated than most households themselves would call ideal.

activities.takeaway: Households who would be perfectly happy as a minority on their street still sort themselves into a city far more segregated than any of them wanted. In these models, tolerance alone does not bring integration. This describes what could happen, not a measurement of what does happen in real cities.

activities.title: How far does the evidence reach?
activities.prompt: Sort each claim by how the sources stand on it.

groups.label: Supported by the models and surveys

cards.text: In Schelling-type models, mild preferences for similar neighbours can produce high segregation with no discrimination at all.
cards.feedback: Supported. Zhang's proofs and the simulations in all four sources show this across many model variants.

cards.text: In the Los Angeles survey, no racial or ethnic group expressed a preference for being a minority in its own neighbourhood.
cards.feedback: Supported. This is a direct survey finding, though it covers stated wishes in one metropolitan area.

cards.text: In these models, removing discrimination alone does not quickly produce integration when preferences are like those in the surveys.
cards.feedback: Supported. The simulations contained no discrimination at all, and segregation still emerged.

cards.text: Preferences are the main cause of segregation in today's US cities.
cards.feedback: Overreach. The authors show preferences cannot be dismissed, but they admit that nonexperimental data cannot separate the effects of preferences from those of discrimination.

cards.text: Discrimination never played a real role in creating segregated neighbourhoods.
cards.feedback: Overreach, and contradicted. Clark and Fossett themselves say past coercion and race-restricted covenants produced involuntary separation.

cards.text: How much of real-world segregation comes from preferences, from discrimination and from income gaps.
cards.feedback: Open. The sources describe a 'contentious debate' that neither side can settle with nonexperimental data. The factors probably combine.

cards.text: Where neighbourhood preferences come from: group identity, stereotypes, practical benefits or fears about home values.
cards.feedback: Open. The paper calls this an ongoing debate and lists many plausible origins. It argues that the origin does not change what the preferences do in the models.

cards.text: Treating the Schelling model like a physics model of magnets deepens our understanding of social segregation.
cards.feedback: Debated. Gauvin and colleagues find the physics tools reveal sharp transitions and a 'tipping' jump. Clark and Fossett reply that the analogy leaves out the social choices that give the model its importance.

activities.takeaway: The models firmly support a possibility: preferences could segregate a city with no discrimination. How much they do so in real cities is not settled, and neither is where the preferences come from.
hints: Ask whether the claim is about what models can do, or about how much something matters in real cities.
Claims with 'main cause' or 'never' need evidence that separates causes, and nonexperimental data cannot do that.

activities.question: Which passage shows the authors admitting that real-city evidence cannot settle how much preferences matter compared with discrimination?

options.quote: Because neither group can establish empirically grounded evaluations of the effects of either preferences or discrimination, recent work has focused on the logical standing of explanations based on social distance
options.feedback: Correct. Neither side can measure the real effects, so the work asks whether a preference explanation is logically possible, not how large its effect is.

options.quote: Thus, high levels of segregation emerge when targets for same-group contact shift from 20% to 40%.
options.feedback: This is a simulation result about what happens inside the model. It says nothing about how preferences and discrimination compare in real cities.

options.quote: Because no group expresses a preference for minority status, no conceivable neighborhood ethnic mix can satisfy the preferences of all groups.
options.feedback: This is a survey-based argument that preferences conflict. It supports the possibility of segregation rather than marking a limit of the evidence.

options.quote: Practices of legal, institutional race exclusion have been substantially dismantled, but stereotypes and prejudice remain and can promote residential separation in the absence of housing discrimination.
options.feedback: This argues that preferences can still matter without discrimination. It makes a claim and admits no limit on measuring it.

hints: Look for a passage about what can and cannot be established with real data.

activities.question: In every surveyed group, a sizeable share of people would accept fewer same-group neighbours. Why, according to Clark and Fossett, don't their choices produce integrated neighbourhoods?

options.text: Each arrival makes a neighbourhood more attractive to the newcomer's group and less attractive to others, so neighbourhoods drift toward sameness unless most people actively avoid being in the majority.
options.feedback: Right. Outcomes come from the sorting process as a whole, not from the most tolerant individuals. The result is more segregated than most households find ideal.

options.text: Discrimination stops the tolerant households from moving where they would like.
options.feedback: This is not the explanation given here. The simulations contained no discrimination, and segregation still emerged.

options.text: The tolerant households secretly hold stronger preferences than they report.
options.feedback: The paper makes no such claim. Its argument works even when the stated preferences are taken at face value.

options.text: The outcome is set by the most tolerant members of each group, and they are too few.
options.feedback: The paper says the opposite: outcomes are not decided by one group's choices, or by the choices of its most tolerant members.

activities.question: A city council member says: 'Once we fully enforce fair-housing law, our neighbourhoods will integrate on their own within a few years.' What do the sources in this lesson support?

options.text: They cast doubt on it. With preferences like those in the surveys, the models drift toward segregation even without discrimination, at least in the short run. They cannot say exactly how this particular city will behave.
options.feedback: Supported. This matches the paper's conclusion that tolerance and the absence of discrimination will not produce integration under current preferences, 'at least, not in the short run'. It also keeps the limits of model evidence in view.

options.text: They prove the council member wrong, because preferences are the main cause of segregation in that city.
options.feedback: Overreach. The models show what preferences could do. They cannot measure how much of any real city's segregation preferences cause.

options.text: They support the claim: once discrimination ends, tolerant households will mix.
options.feedback: Contradicted. Clark and Fossett say formal theory and simulations go against the idea that removing discrimination alone would allow substantial integration.

options.text: They show that enforcing fair-housing law is pointless.
options.feedback: Not supported. The authors say several factors probably act together, and discrimination is illegal with legal remedies. Doubting quick integration is not the same as calling enforcement useless.

hints: Separate two questions: what the models predict, and how much they can say about one real city.
The authors' own conclusion includes the phrase 'at least, not in the short run'.
